exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1 and 2, convert the matrix of observations to mean-deviation form, and construct the sample covariance matrix.

problem.paragraph: Find the principal components of the data for Exercise 1.
Find the principal components of the data for Exercise 2.

[T] A Landsat image with three spectral components was made of Homestead Air Force Base in Florida (after the base was hit by Hurricane Andrew in 1992). The covariance matrix of the data is shown below. Find the first principal component of the data, and compute the percentage of the total variance that is contained in this component. $$S = \left[\right. 164.12 & 32.73 & 81.04 32.73 & 539.44 & 249.13 81.04 & 249.13 & 189.11 \left]\right.$$

[T] The covariance matrix below was obtained from a Landsat image of the Columbia River in Washington, using data from three spectral bands. Let $$x_{1}$$ , $$x_{2}$$ , $$x_{3}$$ denote the spectral components of each pixel in the image. Find a new variable of the form $$y_{1} = c_{1}x_{1} + c_{2}x_{2} + c_{3}x_{3}$$ that has maximum possible variance, subject to the constraint that $$c_{1}^{2} + c_{2}^{2} + c_{3}^{2} = 1$$ . What percentage of the total variance in the data is explained by $$y_{1}$$ ? $$S = \left[\right. 29.64 & 18.38 & 5.00 18.38 & 20.82 & 14.06 5.00 & 14.06 & 29.21 \left]\right.$$

Let $$x_{1},x_{2}$$ denote the variables for the two-dimensional data in Exercise 1. Find a new variable $$y_{1}$$ of the form $$y_{1} = c_{1}x_{1} + c_{2}x_{2}$$ , with $$c_{1}^{2} + c_{2}^{2} = 1,$$ such that $$y_{1}$$ has maximum possible variance over the given data. How much of the variance in the data is explained by $$y_{1}$$ ?
Repeat Exercise 7 for the data in Exercise 2.

Suppose three tests are administered to a random sample of college students. Let $$\textbf{X}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{X}_{N}$$ be observation vectors in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that list the three scores of each student, and for $$j = 1,2,3$$ , let $$x_{j}$$ denote a student’s score on the $$j \text{th}$$ exam. Suppose the covariance matrix of the data is $$S = \left[\right. 5 & 2 & 0 2 & 6 & 2 0 & 2 & 7 \left]\right.$$

Let $$y$$ be an “index” of student performance, with $$y = c_{1}x_{1} + c_{2}x_{2} + c_{3}x_{3}$$ and $$c_{1}^{2} + c_{2}^{2} + c_{3}^{2} = 1.$$ Choose $$c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$$ so that the variance of $$y$$ over the data set is as large as possible. [Hint: The eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix are $$\text{λ} = 3,6$$ , and $$9$$ .]
[T] Repeat Exercise 9 with $$S = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 5 & 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 11 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

Given multivariate data $$\textbf{X}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{X}_{N}$$ (in $$\left. \mathbb{R}^{p} \right)$$ in mean-deviation form, let $$P$$ be a $$p \times p$$ matrix, and define $$\textbf{Y}_{k} = P^{T}\textbf{X}_{k}$$ for $$k = 1,\ldots,N$$ .

list.item: Show that $$\textbf{Y}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{Y}_{N}$$ are in mean-deviation form. [Hint: Let $$\textbf{w}$$ be the vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{N}$$ with a $$1$$ in each entry. Then $$\left\lbrack {\textbf{X}_{1} \cdots \textbf{X}_{N}} \right\rbrack\textbf{w} = 0$$ (the zero vector in $$\left. \mathbb{R}^{p} \right)$$ .]
Show that if the covariance matrix of $$\textbf{X}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{X}_{N}$$ is $$S$$ , then the covariance matrix of $$\textbf{Y}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{Y}_{N}$$ is $$P^{T}SP$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{X}$$ denote a vector that varies over the columns of a $$p \times N$$ matrix of observations, and let $$P$$ be a $$p \times p$$ orthogonal matrix. Show that the change of variable $$\textbf{X} = P\textbf{Y}$$ does not change the total variance of the data. [Hint: By Exercise 11, it suffices to show that $$\text{tr} (P^{T}SP) = \text{tr} (S)$$ . Use a property of the trace mentioned in Exercise 27 in Section 5.4.]

list.item: Show how the sample covariance matrix, $$S$$ , defined prior to Example 3, may be written in a form similar to (1). [Hint: Use partitioned matrix multiplication to write $$S$$ as $$1/(N - 1)$$ times the sum of $$N$$ matrices of size $$p \times p$$ . For $$1 \leq k \leq N$$ , write $$\textbf{X}_{k} - \textbf{M}$$ in place of $${\widehat{\textbf{X}}}_{k}$$ .]

problem.paragraph: First arrange the data in mean-deviation form. The sample mean vector is easily seen to be $$\textbf{M} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 130 \\ 65 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Subtract $$\textbf{M}$$ from the observation vectors (the columns in the table) and obtain $$B = \begin{bmatrix} - 10 & - 5 & - 5 & 5 & 15 \\ - 4 & - 5 & - 1 & 3 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$$

Then the sample covariance matrix is $$S & = \frac{1}{5 - 1} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 10 & - 5 & - 5 & 5 & 15 \\ - 4 & - 5 & - 1 & 3 & 7\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 10 & - 4 \\ - 5 & - 5 \\ - 5 & - 1 \\ 5 & 3 \\ 15 & 7\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = \frac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}400 & 190 \\ 190 & 100\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}100.0 & 47.5 \\ 47.5 & 25.0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$
The eigenvalues of $$S$$ are (to two decimal places) $$\lambda_{1} = 123.02 \text{and} \lambda_{2} = 1.98$$

The unit eigenvector corresponding to $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ is $$\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} .900 \\ .436 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . (Since $$S$$ is $$2 \times 2$$ , the computations can be done by hand if a matrix program is not available.) For the size index, set $$y = .900 \hat{w} + .436 \hat{h}$$

where $$\widehat{w}$$ and $$\widehat{h}$$ are weight and height, respectively, in mean-deviation form. The variance of this index over the data set is $$123.02$$ . Because the total variance is $$\text{tr} (S) = 100 + 25 = 125,$$ the size index accounts for practically all $$(98.4\%)$$ of the variance of the data.

The original data for Practice Problem 1 and the line determined by the first principal component $$\textbf{u}$$ are shown in Figure 4. (In parametric vector form, the line is $$\textbf{x} = \textbf{M} + t\textbf{u}$$ .) It can be shown that the line is the best approximation to the data, in the sense that the sum of the squares of the orthogonal distances to the line is minimized. In fact, principal component analysis is equivalent to what is termed orthogonal regression, but that is a story for another day.
